aisBaselineNote: transitsBaseline is withheld (null) until 72 hourly samples exist on the current tiled12-active30m basis. The basis reset on 2026-07-30, when the AIS scraper stopped taking one thinned request for the whole bounding box and began tiling it so each tile is saturated, stepping counts up roughly 3.4x on total; the median is withheld again until enough post-cutover samples build up, the same as it was for roughly 3 days after the first cutover on 2026-07-20. Samples on an earlier basis are not mixed in. It is an AIS concurrent-presence median, a different population from transits.baseline (IMF PortWatch daily crossings); do not divide one by the other.
aisFirstFixNote: aisConcurrentInZone counts only vessels whose movement was measured against an earlier position. aisFirstFixInZone counts vessels seen in the same window for the first time, which have nothing to compare against yet; they are in neither aisConcurrentInZone nor stranded.

aisGaps.countScope: count is a floor on hulls we stopped receiving, not a count of evasions. Read it against eligibleTankers, the screened tanker population, and against ambientDarkRate, the share of eligible non-tankers that went dark on the identical test. The tanker rate (35.5%) is running 2.2x the ambient rate (16.5%), a gap too large to read as ambient dropout alone.
aisGaps.vesselsTrackedScope: vesselsTracked is a cumulative, all-time, all-type total (every vessel ever recorded anywhere in the wider AIS bbox). It is not the screened population behind count: that population is tankers only, with 50 or more sightings, last seen inside the core area.

capeSnapshot.note: transitsLast24h counts port arrivals only (departures are not published upstream), across ports on both sides of the strait. Not a Hormuz crossing count. Use transits.count for that. An arrival is a port-area entry event rather than a distinct hull: adjacent ports double count and an anchorage reposition can re-trigger one, so read arrivals24hTotal as an activity index. expectedTotal is a 30-day forward book (ships expected within the next 30 days), not a queue waiting now. This feed is retired: the upstream port pages moved these aggregates behind a subscription on 2026-08-28 and have published none since, so the figures are frozen at asOf. For live Hormuz-corridor port activity use /api/v1/ports; for live Cape traffic use the cape row in chokepoints above.

carrierSuspensions.notes: Mediterranean Shipping Company routes Asia–Europe services via the Cape of Good Hope. Its March advisory suspended Middle East bookings and told ships in the area to shelter; it has published no vessel count since.

Maersk has suspended bookings to Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Gulf ports, Jordan and most UAE ports. It discharges at Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, outside the strait, and moves cargo overland to Jebel Ali, and it charges USD 1,000 a container on any vessel that transits the Strait of Hormuz. It said on 25 June that three of its vessels remained in the Gulf.

CMA CGM has activated Cape of Good Hope routing for all Asia–Europe services. Its chief financial officer said on the second-quarter earnings call on 30 July that eight of its vessels were inside the Gulf and unable to exit through the strait.
carrierSuspensions.sourceName: CMA CGM Q2 earnings call, via WorldCargo News

carrierSuspensions.notes: COSCO Shipping has suspended bookings to Bandar Abbas and routes Europe-bound services via the Cape. Two of its container ships crossed the strait in late March with Iranian clearance; it has not published a Gulf posture or vessel count since.
Hapag-Lloyd has suspended Hormuz transits and reroutes via the Cape. By 1 July it had moved all four of its vessels out of the Gulf.
Ocean Network Express suspended new bookings to and from the Persian Gulf on 2 March 2026, citing safety for crew, vessels and cargo. No advisory newer than that has been found.
carrierSuspensions.sourceName: ONE · Temporary Suspension of Bookings to and from the Persian Gulf, 2 March 2026

carrierSuspensions.notes: Evergreen Marine suspended new bookings to Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia (except Jeddah) and Iraq's Umm Qasr port on 5 March 2026, citing crew and vessel safety. No advisory newer than that has been found.
carrierSuspensions.sourceName: Container News, 5 March 2026, citing Evergreen Marine advisory

carrierSuspensions.notes: HMM declared a service deviation for cargo linked to the Arabian Gulf, Red Sea and Horn of Africa on 13 March 2026 and said it would invoke its bill of lading rights over affected shipments. No advisory newer than that has been found.

carrierSuspensions.notes: Yang Ming revised its GS2 service on 26 March 2026 and said on 20 April that ships bound for Middle East ports beyond Sohar, Oman would discharge at Khor Fakkan instead, with normal routing to resume once conditions allow. No advisory newer than that has been found.

chokepointsNote: preCrisisBaselineMedian on every row is computed over one fixed window (baselineWindowStart to baselineWindowEnd) anchored to the Hormuz crisis. For hormuz that window is a genuine pre-crisis baseline. For bab-el-mandeb, suez and cape it is not: those routes were already carrying diverted Red Sea traffic within that window, so preCrisisBaselineMedian for those rows reads as wartime volume, not a peacetime figure.

bullets: Al Jazeera reports US and Iran held mediated UNGA talks on ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff involved.

Per Iranian state media, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi presented Tehran's conditions for reopening the strait at the New York UNGA meeting; The Guardian reports Iran floated a seven-day reopening timeline, subject to conditions.

dailyBrief.summary: The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to commercial traffic, with IMF PortWatch recording 1 transit on 2026-09-20 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day. The dominant development in this window is diplomatic: NewsCord reports that US and Iranian officials held mediated talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with both the ongoing war and the strait's reopening on the agenda, and Al Jazeera names US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as the mediator. Per Iranian state media, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi presented Tehran's conditions for reopening the strait at that New York meeting. The Guardian reports Iran floated a seven-day reopening timeline, subject to conditions, a claim consistent with the parliament speaker's previously stated requirements covering sanctions, the blockade, and frozen assets. Separately, Al Jazeera and gCaptain report Italy and Iran have discussed talks to reopen the strait, and gCaptain reports Trump escalated rhetoric toward Iran even as the US pursued a Hormuz deal at the UN. On the ground in Yemen, The Guardian reports up to 169 people killed over three days as Iran-aligned Houthis battle Saudi-backed forces for Red Sea coastal territory. The Shandong Redwoo, a Bermuda-flagged LNG tanker first tracked in this feed on 2026-09-22, crossed the strait en route to Karachi, per Hellenic Shipping News. Brent stood at $100.44, up 1.60% over 24 hours, as of 11:49 UTC. As of 11:49 UTC, 336 AIS-visible vessels were holding position away from berth in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf watch box, a count that leaves out ships within 25km of a working port. On the Hormuz Index, Crisis Pressure, the state composite, sits in the extreme band, with its value set by physical transit deviation alone; the Escalation Forecast sits in the elevated band, with the Brent-WTI forward spread as its top contributor.

narrative.summary: The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to commercial traffic since February 28, 2026. Iran re-declared it closed after the July ceasefire collapsed, and the war has spread to a second chokepoint, where Yemen's Houthis now hold the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb. US forces have destroyed Iranian tankers and Iran has fired missiles at US warships and bases, while merchant ships are still being hit: the tanker El Gaia burned off Oman with crew missing, and Iran says it struck and detained a Togo-flagged tanker on September 17 for crossing without its permission. Drones launched from Iraq shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the largest route around the strait, on September 11; Reuters and Bloomberg report a low-rate restart on September 22 that Saudi Aramco has not confirmed. How much is moving is now contested: US Central Command says it has escorted more than a billion barrels out in two months and that volumes are at a six-month high, while independent trackers and our own count still show a handful of crossings a day, two on September 21 by Kpler's count. On September 22 an Iranian official told Reuters that Iran could reopen the strait within seven days if Washington lifted its blockade, but Iranian state media called that untrue, and the parliament speaker says the strait stays shut until the blockade and oil sanctions are lifted and Tehran's frozen assets released.

pipelineBypass.name: Petroline (East-West Pipeline)
pipelineBypass.notes: Saudi Aramco's East-West Pipeline carries Arabian Light from Abqaiq to Yanbu on the Red Sea, the single largest non-Hormuz route for Gulf crude. Saudi Arabia shut it as a precaution on 11 September 2026 after drones launched from Iraq struck it in the Riyadh and Medina areas, damaging pipeline equipment. It had been carrying 4 to 5 million barrels a day, close to all of the Saudi crude rerouted away from the strait. On 22 September, Reuters and Bloomberg, citing industry sources, reported a restart at a low pumping rate with a target of about 4 million barrels a day. Saudi Aramco and the energy ministry have not confirmed it, so this row stays offline until a restart or a flow figure is confirmed.
pipelineBypass.sourceName: EIA · World Oil Transit Chokepoints, Al Jazeera, CNN

pipelineBypass.name: ADCOP (Habshan-Fujairah)
pipelineBypass.notes: ADNOC's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline lifts UAE crude past the Strait of Hormuz to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, where it loads on tankers transiting the open Indian Ocean.

pipelineBypass.name: Goreh-Jask Pipeline
pipelineBypass.notes: Iran's pipeline from the southwest oilfields to Jask on the Gulf of Oman bypasses the Strait, but throughput remains a fraction of nameplate capacity.

premium.note: Machine-payable premium endpoints (x402, USDC on Base): full vessel manifest with sanctions cross-reference, hourly history capped at one year with actual depth growing daily, one-call snapshot, structured daily brief, single-vessel dossiers, bulk export, real-time streaming, threshold-alert webhooks, a Hormuz flag rollup, a shadow-fleet risk screen of the vessels active on AIS in the Persian Gulf window, bunker and marine-fuel prices, and a modeled war-risk premium nowcast. $0.01-$0.50 per request, no key or account. MCP connector at the mcp URL.

strandedNote: `stranded` counts every vessel not under way anywhere in the watch box, including ones at berth working cargo at regional ports such as Dubai and Abu Dhabi. `strandedOffshore` excludes vessels within 25km of a working port and is the narrower figure the site's own narrative uses.

transits.cadenceNote: Completed daily transits (IMF PortWatch crossing count). Not the same as aisConcurrentInZone, which is a snapshot of vessels moving inside the wider Persian Gulf watch box right now, not the Strait channel itself.
transits.freshestDayNote: The newest PortWatch row is always a Sunday, because IMF publishes weekly on Tuesday against data carrying a ~2-day lag. Sunday is the lowest-traffic weekday in this series, so the freshest print reads low against the day before it even in a normal week. Compare it with earlier Sundays, or with baselineMedian, rather than with previousNTotal.

verdict.long: War-risk insurance has priced commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz beyond the reach of most operators.
